pages.text:
*Jun's phone says: 0%, screen dark. Nari's river says: calm; someone is waiting.*

The man was not fishing. He sat on the wet concrete with his legs crossed, holding a long rod that dipped low into the water. He wore a wide-brimmed hat and a vest with so many pockets it looked like a beehive. When the pear-green boat bumped gently against the pier, he did not jump. He simply turned his head, slowly, tracking the light.

"Good morning," said Jun. His voice sounded thin in the quiet air.

The man looked at the two orange life vests. He looked at the muddy white sneakers. He looked at the wooden plank that had served as a paddle. Then he looked at their faces, which were pale and tired and still holding on to each other.

"Aigoo," he said. It was not a shout. It was a soft, heavy sound, like a bag of grain being set down carefully on a table.

"Are you lost?" the man asked. His voice was dry and cheerful, completely out of place with the grey sky.

"We are found," said Nari. She was still gripping the gunwale. Her knuckles were white.

"Found is good," the man said. "Lost is bad. Come. The corn is almost ready."
pages.image: Mr. Cho, in his khaki fishing vest and wide-brimmed hat, sits on a concrete pier seen from behind and looks down at Jun and Nari, two tired children in orange life vests, sitting in the green boat beside the pier.

pages.text:
He hauled the boat to the edge of the pier with one strong pull, then reached down a thick arm to lift Jun out first. Jun’s wet sneakers slapped the concrete as Nari landed with a small thump, immediately straightening her braid.

"Are you hurt?" the man asked. It was not a question that needed an answer, but it was the right one to ask in the damp quiet.

"No," said Jun.

"No," said Nari.

"Good," said the man. "Are you hungry?"

Jun opened his mouth, closed it, and looked at Nari, who was already staring at the man with the intensity of a cat watching a mouse hole.

"Yes," they said at the same time.

The man nodded and led them past a small shed where a gas burner hissed under a dented pot. Steam rose into the air, carrying the sweet, starch-heavy smell of corn. The rain had stopped, but the world still felt thick and heavy.

"Sit," the man said, pointing to a wooden bench under the shed’s overhang. "I am Mr. Cho. I wait for the fish, and the fish do not come. I wait for you, and you came."
pages.image: Mr. Cho, in his khaki fishing vest and wide-brimmed hat, lifts Jun out of the green boat onto a concrete pier while Nari in her orange life vest waits in the boat; a small shed with a steaming pot behind them.

pages.text:
Jun sat on the bench, his legs dangling over the edge while the wood warmed the backs of his legs. Nari settled beside him, close enough that their shoulders touched, and she did not pull away.

"My name is Jun," he said, the words tumbling out like a dam breaking. "I am from Seoul. I live on the fourteenth floor. I go to hagwon every day, even when I do not want to." He took a breath. "This is my cousin, Nari. She lives here. In the village. With her grandmother, who is also my grandmother. And her grandfather, who is also my grandfather. They have a big farm. With peppers."

Nari leaned in, correcting him with the precision of a teacher marking a test. "The farm is the Choi family farm. And the boat is the Pear."

Mr. Cho nodded, as if he had been expecting this exact conversation for a long time. "The one who says four words a year?"

Nari raised her head, her eyes sharp. "Five. He says 'Stay with the boat.' That is one. He says 'Eat.' That is two. He says 'Good.' That is three. He says 'Aigoo.' That is four. And he says 'Go.' That is five."

Jun pushed his glasses up his nose. A strange, warm pride settled in his chest, not because he was right, but because Nari was so specific, and he liked that.
pages.image: Jun and Nari, both in orange life vests, sit on a wooden bench under a shed roof while Mr. Cho, in his wide-brimmed hat, watches them with a gentle smile near a steaming pot.

pages.text:
Mr. Cho reached into his many-pocketed vest and pulled out a phone with a cracked screen, older than anything Jun had ever seen. He dialed a number and held it to his ear.

"Hello? It is Mr. Cho. I have the cousins. They are here. They are... safe."

He listened, then held the device out to Jun. The boy took it with both hands, a habit Halmoni had drilled into him.

"Uncle," he said, his voice sounding tiny in the quiet air.

A voice on the other end broke. It was not loud, but it was cracked, like a dry twig snapping in the wind. Then there was silence, and from a long way away, Uncle’s voice came through, clear and hard and shaking.

"Are they there? Are they whole?"

Mr. Cho took the phone back and looked at Nari. "Your father wants to talk."

Nari took it. She held it to her ear, closing her eyes as she listened to the breathing on the other end, the sound of a man who had been running, waiting, and afraid.

"Appa," she whispered.

She could not manage anything else, so she just held the phone tighter, her shoulders trembling just a little.
pages.image: Nari, with her long black braid, holds a phone to her ear with a tearful expression while Jun, in his glasses, sits beside her, both wearing orange life vests on a wet pier.

pages.text:
The corn arrived in a large metal bowl, still steaming, the bright yellow kernels glistening in the dim light. Mr. Cho handed them a blanket each, thick wool that smelled of camphor and old wood. They wrapped themselves up, huddled together against the cool air.

Jun bit into a kernel. It was sweet and hot and real. He chewed slowly, looking down at his feet. His white sneakers were brown now, splattered with mud from the river, the sandbar, and the journey. He had been so worried about them getting dirty, about being clean, and being right, and being perfect.

Now they were just shoes. Muddy, warm, and safe.

"My phone died," Jun said softly.

Nari bit into her corn. She looked at him, her eyes bright.

"Good," she said. "Now we're even."

And Jun did not mind at all that his phone was dead. He just sat there, in the drizzle, with the person who knew the river. The worry lifted, just a little, like a heavy backpack finally set down on the grass.
pages.image: Jun and Nari, wrapped in thick wool blankets and wearing orange life vests, eat hot corn kernels together on a wooden bench under a shed roof in the rain.
